rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its headline, "A 22% drop in no-shows: what Mindbody's AI pilot proves and what it doesn't," is exactly the right posture: use the number, then make the methodology earn it. B is strong, but "The software behind 50,000 studios wants AI to solve fitness's empty-slot problem" smuggles in a market thesis the update does not prove. That is how a decent angle gets dressed up and starts lying by implication.
gaps_in_A: "The scheduling half of the product, where the assistant suggests class times from booking data, belongs in this same story" risks cramming two product behaviors into one operator feature before proving a named studio used both.
"what the company's owners expect from it" leans past the supplied facts; the update says take-private, not owner strategy or owner expectations.
"a small-business columnist at a regional business outlet" needs a local named studio to be real; without geography, that target is a little airy.
gaps_in_B: "most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is an invented market claim. Maybe true, maybe not; it is not in the update.
"fitness's empty-slot problem" overstates the evidence. You have a pilot no-show claim, not proof of an industry-wide empty-slot problem.
"The prevailing pattern that reporter is tracking is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" imports a trend claim without evidence, then builds the contrarian angle on top of it.
"Not for fitness trades, who don't cover SaaS pricing strategy" is too absolute. Fitness-business trades absolutely care what studio software costs if the pricing affects operators.
